## What this project is trying to answer

We want to know how well psychology studies published in the journal *PLOS ONE*
report the **demographics of the people they study** — the participants' gender,
race, education, and socioeconomic status — and whether that reporting has
**changed over time**, from 2010 through 2026.

The bigger question behind this is representativeness: if researchers don't
report who their participants are, we can't tell whether findings generalize
beyond a narrow slice of the population. Tracking reporting habits year by year
tells us whether the field is improving.

To do this at scale, we can't read tens of thousands of papers by hand. So the
plan is to have a large language model (an AI system) read each paper's methods
section and pull out the demographic details into a spreadsheet we can analyze.

We split the work into four time periods for comparison:

| Stage | Years | Why |
|-------|-------|-----|
| Early | 2010–2014 | Baseline |
| Middle | 2015–2019 | Pre-pandemic |
| COVID | 2020–2023 | Pandemic era |
| Post-COVID | 2024–2026 | Recovery |

## How the pipeline works, in plain terms

Think of it as an assembly line. Each stage hands its output to the next:

```
Find the psychology papers  →  Pick a small test batch  →  Have the AI read them
        (done)                       (done)                    (next step)
        →  Check the AI's accuracy  →  Run it on all ~55,000 papers  →  Analyze trends
```

We are currently at the end of stage two: we have the full list of papers and a
small pilot batch ready for the AI to test on.

## Three decisions we had to make up front

**1. Where do we get the papers?** PLOS publishes all its articles, and there
are two ways in: download every article as a file (a project called
*allofplos*), or query PLOS's search engine (called *Solr*). We ended up using
**both** — the search engine to *find* the right papers, and the downloaded
files to *read* their full text. (More on why below — this took some
detective work.)

**2. How do we pick a test batch?** Before trusting the AI on 55,000 papers, we
test it on a handful and check its work by hand. We pick **2 papers from each
psychology subfield** so the test covers the whole range of topics, not just the
most common ones.

**3. Which AI model?** We chose **Llama 3.3 (70B)** — a large, accurate
open model — over a smaller, cheaper alternative. Because we're running on the
university's supercomputer (Rivanna), the cost of the bigger model isn't a
concern, and accuracy matters most: a missed or made-up demographic number would
distort the whole analysis.

## Getting the data: a detour worth documenting

This is where the project got interesting. Our first plan was to download every
PLOS article and read each one's built-in subject labels to find the psychology
papers. Every article is tagged by PLOS with topics like
"Biology → Psychology → Social psychology."

We wrote code to read those tags:

```python
# Simplified: find the psychology subfield an article is tagged with
def get_psychology_subfields(article):
    # PLOS nests tags like:  Psychology > Social psychology
    # We grab the specific subfield sitting under "Psychology"
    ...
    return subfields   # e.g. ["Social psychology"]
```

When we ran this across all 391,000 downloaded articles, it worked — but a
routine sanity check turned up something odd. Counting the psychology papers we
found per year:

```
2014: 2,002 papers
2015:    12 papers   ← almost nothing?!
2016: 2,100 papers
```

**The year 2015 had almost no psychology papers.** That's not believable — 2015
was a normal year. Something was wrong.

Digging in, we found the cause: for about **99% of 2015 articles, the downloaded
files simply don't contain the subject tags at all**. PLOS applied those tags on
their website but never embedded them in the files for that period. No amount of
clever code can read a label that isn't there. Losing 2015 would have gutted our
"Middle" time period.

The fix: PLOS's **search engine does have the tags for every article**, even the
ones missing from the files. So we switched to asking PLOS's search engine
directly: "give me every PLOS ONE psychology research article from 2010 to
2026." One important lesson learned — the query needs a specific setting
(`doc_type:full`) or it returns millions of irrelevant fragments:

```bash
# Ask PLOS's search engine for 2015 psychology papers
curl 'https://api.plos.org/search?q=*:*&fq=doc_type:full&fq=journal:"PLOS ONE"
      &fq=article_type:"Research Article"&fq=subject:"Psychology"
      &fq=publication_date:[2015-01-01T00:00:00Z TO 2015-12-31T23:59:59Z]'
```

That query returned **4,346 psychology papers for 2015** — the year that had
looked empty. Problem solved, and we still use the downloaded files for the one
thing they're reliable for: the full text the AI needs to read.

## The finished article list

After switching to the search engine, the numbers look healthy across every
year — no gaps:

```python
total: 58,467 psychology articles
by year:
  2010:  853   2014: 4,249   2018: 3,492   2022: 3,761
  2011: 1,886  2015: 4,346   2019: 3,219   2023: 3,761
  2012: 2,481  2016: 3,663   2020: 3,548   2024: 4,249
  2013: 4,478  2017: 3,367   2021: 3,714   2025: 5,009
by stage:
  early: 13,947   middle: 18,087   covid: 14,784   post-covid: 11,649
```

(2010 is genuinely smaller because PLOS ONE was younger then — that's a real
trend, not an error.) About 6% of these are very recent papers we don't yet have
the full text for, so those are set aside for the reading step.

## The pilot test batch

Finally, we drew the small batch to test the AI on. We take 2 papers from each
psychology subfield PLOS uses, chosen at random but with a fixed "seed" so the
selection is reproducible — anyone re-running it gets the exact same 46 papers:

```bash
python -m src.sample_articles --index data/corpus_index.csv \
                              --out data/sampled_articles.csv
```

Result: **46 papers spanning 23 subfields** — Social psychology, Cognitive
psychology, Developmental psychology, Personality, Emotions, Psychometrics, and
more. This is the batch we'll use to check the AI's accuracy before committing to
all 55,000.

## What happens next

1. **Run the pilot** — have Llama 3.3 read the 46 test papers and extract their
   demographic details.
2. **Check its work by hand** against a scoring guide (did it catch every
   reported group? Are the percentages right?).
3. **Run the full extraction** on all ~55,000 papers (split across the
   supercomputer's GPUs).
4. **Analyze the trends** — reporting rates for gender, race, education, and
   socioeconomic status, year by year and across the four time periods. This is
   the answer to the original question.
